Enquiry 1: Ice Age Hunters & Sunken Doggerland — How Did Stone Age People Survive? (c. 800,000–4000 BC)

Big Question: How did Old and Middle Stone Age hunter-gatherers survive in Britain, and how did Britain become an island?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Prehistory (Pre-his-to-ry) Palaeolithic (Pa-lae-o-lith-ic) Knapping (Knap-ping) Mesolithic (Mes-o-lith-ic) Doggerland (Dog-ger-land)
TASK 1 Archaeological Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Tear-Drop Chipped Flint Handaxe (c. 400,000 BC)
Archaeology Clue: With zero written books in prehistory, flaked flint handaxes prove early humans shaped sharp multi-purpose tools hundreds of thousands of years ago!

1a. Look closely at the chipped edges on Source A. How was it made, and what jobs did it do?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, Palaeolithic hunters chipped sharp teardrop flint handaxes like this so they could..."
Word Bank: flint knapping • tear-drop blade • butcher meat • scrape hides
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Mesolithic families build wooden huts and carve deer-antler masks at Star Carr (c. 9000 BC)
Early humans leave footprints in mud at Happisburgh in Norfolk (c. 850,000 BC)
Melting ice floods Doggerland and turns Britain into an island (c. 6500 BC)
Ice Age hunters shelter in limestone caves at Creswell Crags (c. 40,000–12,000 BC)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events changed people's lives the most, and why?

Explain what Doggerland was and why Britain became an island around 6500 BC.

Starter: "During the Ice Age and early Mesolithic, Britain was not an island yet because..." • Word Bank: Doggerland • land bridge • 6500 BC • North Sea
TASK 4 "Thinking Heads" • Two Different Viewpoints

How do flint handaxes, animal furs, and caves help your family survive freezing winters?
🗣 Person B: Mesolithic Hunter at Star Carr

Starter: "Between the icy Palaeolithic and the warmer Mesolithic, Stone Age life in Britain changed hugely..."

Enquiry 2: The First Farmers & Skara Brae — How Did Farming Change Stone Age Life? (c. 4000–2500 BC)

Big Question: How did farming transform everyday Stone Age life, and what does Skara Brae reveal about Neolithic homes?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Neolithic (Ne-o-lith-ic) Agriculture (Ag-ri-cul-ture) Sickle (Sick-le) Skara Brae (Ska-ra Brae) Long Barrow (Long Bar-row)
TASK 1 Archaeological Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Stone Box Beds, Central Hearth & Flagstone Walls at Skara Brae, Orkney (c. 3100–2500 BC)
Orkney Storm Clue (1850): Buried under sand dunes for over 4,000 years, Skara Brae’s flat sandstone cupboards, beds, and drains survived completely intact.

1a. Spot three pieces of indoor stone furniture in Source A. How did families stay warm inside?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, the stone dresser and walls inside Skara Brae show Neolithic families..."
Word Bank: stone box beds • central hearth • stone dresser • heather and peat
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
A fierce winter storm blows sand dunes away to reveal Skara Brae (AD 1850)
First Neolithic farmers bring wheat, barley, sheep, and cattle across the Channel (c. 4000 BC)
Villagers build stone houses with dressers and beds at Skara Brae in Orkney (c. 3100 BC)
Communities build stone ancestor tombs like West Kennet Long Barrow (c. 3650 BC)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events changed people's lives the most, and why?

✂ Trim along border if sticking into A4 exercise books • The History Revision Hub Page 5 of 16

TASK 3 Historical Investigation • Change, Cause & Consequence

Explain how the arrival of farming around 4000 BC changed how Stone Age people got food and shelter.

Starter: "When Neolithic farming arrived across the sea around 4000 BC, everyday life changed completely because..." • Word Bank: Neolithic • wheat and barley • sheep and cattle • permanent villages
TASK 4 "Thinking Heads" • Two Different Viewpoints
🗣 Person A: Mobile Woodland Forager
Why do you prefer following wild deer, fish, and hazelnuts through the forest?
🗣 Person B: Skara Brae Farmer in Orkney

TASK 5 Mission Challenge • Answer Today's Big Enquiry Question

How did farming transform everyday Stone Age life, and what does Skara Brae reveal about Neolithic homes?

Starter: "Historians view the switch to Neolithic farming around 4000 BC as a giant turning point because..."
Historian Word Bank: agriculture • polished axes • Skara Brae • West Kennet Long Barrow

Enquiry 3: Secrets of Stonehenge — How & Why Did Neolithic People Raise Giant Stones? (c. 3000–2200 BC)

Big Question: How did Neolithic communities build Stonehenge without wheels or metal, and why was it aligned with the sun?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Henge (Henge) Bluestones (Blue-stones) Sarsen (Sar-sen) Trilithon (Tri-li-thon) Solstice (Sol-stice)
TASK 1 Archaeological Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: 1928 Aerial Photograph Showing the Circular Earth Bank and Ditch Around Stonehenge (c. 3000 BC earthwork (1928 photograph))
Engineering Clue: Without cranes, wheels, or metal tools, Neolithic masons pounded stone mortise holes and tenon pegs to lock 7-tonne lintels safely overhead!

1a. Look beyond the centre stones in Source A. What giant outer shape can you spot in the grass?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, an aerial view of Stonehenge reveals a giant circular henge ditch and bank that..."
Word Bank: circular ditch • chalk bank • henge • Heel Stone Avenue
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Spotted bluestones arrive 150 miles from Wales and 25-tonne sarsens are raised (c. 2500 BC)
Workers dig Stonehenge’s circular chalk ditch and bank with deer-antler picks (c. 3000 BC)
Royal Air Force aerial photos reveal buried prehistoric avenues around Stonehenge (AD 1928)
Families travel across Britain for midwinter feasts at Durrington Walls (c. 2500–2400 BC)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events changed people's lives the most, and why?

Enquiry 4: Enter the Bronze Age — How Did Metal & Beaker People Change Britain? (c. 2500–1200 BC)

Big Question: How did Beaker newcomers and bronze metalworking transform life and power in Britain?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Beaker (Bea-ker) Smelting (Smelt-ing) Bronze (Bronze) Mould (Mould) Lunula (Lu-nu-la)
TASK 1 Archaeological Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Decorated Bell Beaker Clay Vessels & Early Bronze Blades (c. 2400–1900 BC)
Science Clue (2002): Oxygen-isotope tests on the Amesbury Archer’s tooth enamel proved he drank icy mountain water near the Alps in central Europe as a boy!

1a. Look closely at Source A. What clues show how skilled Beaker craftworkers were with both clay and metal?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, the patterned clay beakers and metal blades prove Beaker craftworkers could..."
Word Bank: Bell Beaker pots • geometric patterns • bronze blades • smelting
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Archaeologists excavate the Amesbury Archer three miles from Stonehenge (AD 2002)
Bell Beaker newcomers cross from Europe bringing copper and gold working (c. 2450 BC)
Miners dig copper at Great Orme and smiths hammer the Mold Gold Cape (c. 1900–1600 BC)
The Amesbury Archer (raised near the Alps) is buried with 100+ items (c. 2300 BC)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events changed people's lives the most, and why?

Enquiry 5: "Britain's Pompeii" — What Does Must Farm Reveal About Everyday Bronze Age Life? (c. 1200–800 BC)

Big Question: Why do archaeologists call Must Farm "Britain's Pompeii", and what does it reveal about Bronze Age life?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Stilts (Stilts) Causeway (Cause-way) Waterlogged (Wa-ter-logged) Wicker (Wick-er) Sewn-plank boat (Sewn-plank boat)
TASK 1 Archaeological Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Hafted Bronze Axes & Spearhead Excavated at Must Farm, Cambridgeshire (c. 900 BC)
Fenland Mud Clue: Wet, oxygen-free river silt beneath Must Farm stopped rot bacteria—saving wooden handles, Britain’s oldest wheel, woven cloth, and porridge!

1a. Look closely at Source A. Why was finding wooden handles still attached to bronze blades so exciting?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, finding wooden handles still attached to Must Farm’s bronze axes was exciting because..."
Word Bank: wooden handles • bronze sockets • airless river mud • Must Farm
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Archaeologists excavate "Britain’s Pompeii" at Must Farm in Cambridgeshire (AD 2015–2016)
Boatbuilders stitch thick oak planks with yew branches for the Dover Boat (c. 1550 BC)
Fire sweeps Must Farm stilt village, dropping bowls and wheels into mud (c. 850 BC)
Communities build the Flag Fen timber causeway and offer bronze shields in water (c. 1300–900 BC)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events changed people's lives the most, and why?

Enquiry 6: Iron Age Celts & Giant Hillforts — How Did Iron Transform Tribal Britain? (c. 800 BC–AD 43)

Big Question: How did iron tools, hillforts, and Celtic craftwork transform Britain before the Romans arrived in AD 43?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Iron ore (I-ron ore) Rotary quern (Ro-ta-ry quern) Roundhouse (Round-house) Hillfort (Hill-fort) Torc (Torc)
TASK 1 Archaeological Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Spinning Iron Age Rotary Quern Stone for Grinding Grain (Portable Antiquities Scheme) (c. 200 BC–AD 43)
Scale Clue: Maiden Castle’s triple chalk ramparts in Dorset enclosed space for 47 football pitches—protecting Celtic roundhouses, workshops, and winter grain.

1a. Look closely at the round stone with a hole in Source A. How did families use it?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, Iron Age families poured grain into the central hole of a rotary quern stone so they could..."
Word Bank: rotary quern • central hole • wooden handle • bread flour
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Emperor Claudius’s Roman legions invade Britain, ending prehistory (AD 43)
Blacksmiths begin smelting common iron ore and hammering strong ploughs (c. 800 BC)
Craftworkers twist Snettisham gold torcs, decorate shields, and mint gold coins (c. 150–50 BC)
Celtic tribes expand giant multi-rampart hillforts like Maiden Castle (c. 450–100 BC)
